editorial:
You follow John Peterson, a man living a quiet life in Southern California with his partner Eric and their adopted daughter. When his aging father Willis arrives from Los Angeles looking for a retirement spot, old wounds reopen. Willis is stubborn, sharp-tongued, and stuck in his ways, and the two clash over everything from family to identity. The movie leans into raw, uncomfortable family drama, so expect tense dinners and painful conversations rather than big action. It feels personal and grounded, like sitting in on a real family argument you cannot look away from.

The acting is the real draw here, especially Lance Henriksen as Willis, who delivers a fierce and heartbreaking performance. Viggo Mortensen, who also directed, keeps things steady and emotional. The pacing is slow and deliberate, which suits the story but may test your patience if you want fast thrills. Pros include powerful performances and honest writing; cons include heavy themes and a bleak tone. This is best for viewers who enjoy character-driven dramas.
endingExplained: In the final scenes, Willis's health takes a serious turn and he is hospitalized. John stays by his father's side despite years of hurt. Willis finally passes away, and John is left to process a complicated mix of grief and relief. The movie closes on John returning to his family, carrying both the pain and the small moments of connection they shared, suggesting that love and resentment can exist side by side.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves character-driven family dramas.
